4195	\subsection{An explicit cyclic-convolution layout}
4196	
4197	To use the source tensor, we first place the ordinary coefficient stream
4198	in its tensor order. Agarwal and Cooley used the Chinese remainder
4199	theorem to convert one cyclic convolution into multidimensional cyclic
4200	convolution~\cite{AgarwalCooley1977}. The following map uses that
4201	algebraic split, with coordinate powers that make the change of order a
4202	sequence of controlled cyclic shifts.
4203	
4204	Let $s_1,\ldots,s_d$ be the pairwise coprime
4205	source lengths, let $S=\prod_i s_i$, and put
4206	\[
4207	 P_i=\prod_{j<i}s_j,\qquad \mu_i=P_i^{-1}\pmod{s_i}.
4208	\]
4209	Here $P_i$ denotes an integer prefix product, not a Fourier-coordinate
4210	permutation.  The assignment
4211	\[
4212	 \Phi:\mathbb C[x]/(x^S-1)\longrightarrow
4213	 \mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/(x_1^{s_1}-1,\ldots,x_d^{s_d}-1),
4214	 \qquad x\longmapsto\prod_i x_i^{\mu_i}
4215	\]
4216	respects $x^S=1$, so it defines an algebra map.  The target monomial
4217	group has size $S$, and the image of $x$ has order $S$, because each
4218	$\mu_i$ is a unit and the $s_i$ are pairwise coprime.  Its powers
4219	therefore run through all target basis monomials exactly once.  Hence
4220	$\Phi$ is an isomorphism and preserves cyclic convolution.
4221	
4222	Every ordinary coefficient index has a unique mixed-radix expression
4223	\[
4224	 k=\sum_{j=1}^d a_jP_j,\qquad 0\le a_j<s_j.
4225	\]
4226	The coordinate of $\Phi(x^k)$ in axis $i$ is
4227	\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangular-crt}
4228	 b_i=a_i+\mu_i\sum_{j<i}a_jP_j\pmod{s_i}.
4229	\end{equation}
4230	Indeed terms with $j>i$ are divisible by $s_i$, and $\mu_iP_i=1$ modulo
4231	$s_i$.  Numerical order of $k$ is lexicographic order of
4232	$(a_d,\ldots,a_1)$.  Insert the padding in one nested scan of the full
4233	box $\prod_i[0,t_i)$ in this lexicographic order, with $a_d$ the
4234	outermost counter and $a_1$ the innermost.  At an address satisfying
4235	$a_i<s_i$ for every $i$, copy the next original coefficient record;
4236	at every other address, write a zero record.  The valid addresses
4237	occur in the original coefficient order, so each record is copied to
4238	its intended mixed-radix address.  To delete the padding after the
4239	inverse axis reorder, use the same enumeration, copying the record at
4240	each valid address and skipping the record at each invalid address.
4241	
4242	Store the nested binary counters consecutively on a fixed work tape.
4243	Their total width is $\sum_i\log_2t_i=\log_2T=O(p)$, and the stored
4244	bounds $s_i$ also have total width $O(p)$.  At each of the $T$
4245	addresses, updating the counters, testing validity, and handling the
4246	$O(p)$-bit record therefore cost $O(p)$ steps, including counter-head
4247	returns.  Each insertion or deletion scan costs $O(Tp)$.
4248	
4249	Now reorder the complete padded axes to $(a_1,\ldots,a_d)$.  In this
4250	physical order, the coordinates with
4251	indices below $i$ precede coordinate $i$.  Update the targets in the
4252	order $i=d,d-1,\ldots,1$ using \eqref{eq:triangular-crt}.  When target
4253	$i$ is updated, none of its lower-index controls has yet changed, so
4254	the offset is computed from the original digits $a_j$ required by the
4255	formula.
4256	
4257	To specify the action on padded addresses, let
4258	\[
4259	 \mathcal P=\prod_i[0,t_i),\qquad \mathcal V=\prod_i[0,s_i)
4260	\]
4261	be sets of integer addresses.  On a fixed control prefix, rotate the
4262	valid target interval $[0,s_i)$ by the offset in
4263	\eqref{eq:triangular-crt} and fix $[s_i,t_i)$.  If any lower-index
4264	control is invalid, use the identity.  This defines a bijection of
4265	$\mathcal P$: for fixed controls and spectators it is a cyclic
4266	permutation of the valid target interval and the identity elsewhere.
4267	Each step preserves $\mathcal V$ and its complement.  Consequently
4268	zero padding remains zero after every step.  An inverse is explicit:
4269	process $i=1,\ldots,d$, subtracting the same expression formed from the
4270	already recovered lower coordinates; then undo the axis reorder and
4271	perform the deletion scan just described.
4272	
4273	Each triangular update is a prefix-controlled cyclic shift.  The
4274	controls precede its target in the current physical order.  For each
4275	prefix, prepare the offset, split the valid target interval into its
4276	two consecutive pieces, and merge those pieces in the opposite order.
4277	Every target position carries its full spectator suffix as a block;
4278	the invalid interval is copied unchanged.  There are at most $T/t_i$
4279	control prefixes for target $i$.  For any fixed setup degree $C$, all
4280	offsets therefore cost $O(dTp^C/r)=o(Tp)$ to prepare, since
4281	$t_i\ge r/2$ and $r$ exceeds every fixed power of $p$.
4282	
4283	The axis widths are $\ell$ or $\ell-1$.  To exchange two adjacent axes
4284	of unequal width, move the longer axis's leading bit outside their
4285	equal-width pair, swap that pair by the proved chunk-swap procedure,
4286	and put the leading bit at its new position.  This adds a fixed number
4287	of linear passes to the equal-width swap cost.  Reversing all axes
4288	uses $O(d^2)$ such moves.  Therefore the map $\Phi$, its inverse, and
4289	their padding operations cost
4290	\[
4291	 O\bigl(Tp\,d^2(1+\ell^\tau)\bigr).
4292	\]
4293	This construction describes payload movement from address $a$ to its
4294	new address.  It is distinct from the operator convention
4295	$(R_cz)_j=z_{cj}$ used for Fourier dilations, which moves a payload
4296	from address $j$ to $c^{-1}j$.

4486	\subsection{The multiplication algorithm}
4487	
4488	The source-transform procedures now supply the three transforms needed
4489	for the radix-digit convolution. Read each stored operand backward from
4490	its least significant end in groups of $b$ bits. This produces the radix-$2^b$ digits
4491	$a_0,\ldots,a_{q-1}$ in increasing coefficient order.  Buffer each
4492	group on a fixed work tape and read it back most significant bit first,
4493	reversing its least-significant-first input order; pad the final short
4494	group with leading zeroes.
4495	For digit $a_j$, write the exact grid numerator
4496	$a_j2^{p-b-2}$ in a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit real word, followed by a zero
4497	$w_{\rm c}$-bit imaginary word. This exponent is nonnegative
4498	because $p=6b$, and the represented value is exactly $a_j2^{-b-2}$.
4499	Append $S-q$ zero coefficient records.  Buffering and ordering the
4500	groups costs $O(n)$, including the one partial group's padding, and
4501	writing the $S$ records costs $O(Sp)$.
4502	Together with the initial count and copies, this input conversion
4503	costs $O(n+Sp)=O(Tp)$; all $n$ input bits, including leading zeroes,
4504	are retained before the final group is padded.
4505	
4506	With these streams prepared, perform the following operations.
4507	\begin{enumerate}
4508	\item Apply the coefficient-address map $\Phi$, with its padded layout, to obtain
4509	source arrays $u,v$.  Their coefficients are exact $p$-bit grid
4510	values of norm less than $1/4$.
4511	\item Compute $\widetilde{\mathscr F}(u)$ and
4512	$\widetilde{\mathscr F}(v)$.
4513	\item Multiply corresponding complex coefficients exactly and truncate
4514	each real and imaginary part toward zero to $p$ fractional bits, writing
4515	the result in the common $w_{\rm c}$-bit component format.
4516	Denote the resulting source array by $z$.
4517	\item Compute $\widetilde{\mathscr F}^{+}(z)$ and multiply its grid
4518	numerators exactly by $S$, retaining the denominator $2^p$ and writing
4519	each component in signed width $w_{\rm c}+b$. Denote the represented
4520	dyadic array by $\widetilde w$.
4521	\item Multiply the grid numerators of $\widetilde w$ exactly by
4522	$2^{2b+4}S$, again retaining the denominator $2^p$, and write each
4523	component in signed width $w_{\rm c}+4b+4$. Round the represented real
4524	values to the nearest integers. At each valid address, write the rounded
4525	coefficient in one signed $(3b+1)$-bit word, most significant bit first;
4526	at every padded address,
4527	write a zero word of that width. Supply this local payload width to
4528	$\Phi^{-1}$ and apply it, including removal of the address padding, to
4529	restore the ordinary coefficient order.
4530	\item Propagate radix-$2^b$ carries in increasing coefficient order.
4531	Write the resulting bits from least to most significant on a work tape,
4532	then reverse that stream and output exactly $2n$ bits in
4533	most-significant-first order.
4534	\end{enumerate}
4535	
4536	The two occurrences of $S$ in this algorithm undo different
4537	normalizations.  By \eqref{eq:source-permutation-cancel}, the exact
4538	counterpart after the three transforms is $(u*v)/S^2$, so after the
4539	first scale it is $w=(u*v)/S$.  The second scale gives
4540	$2^{2b+4}(u*v)$, whose inverse image under $\Phi$ is the original
4541	integer coefficient convolution.  The next subsection verifies the
4542	disk bounds needed by every call and proves that the final error is
4543	less than $1/2$; it also justifies the rounding, carries, and output
4544	length.

4555	\subsubsection{Scales and disk margins}
4556	
4557	Put $h_p=2^{-p}$, and use the coefficient sup norm throughout this
4558	subsection.  An error of $a$ will mean absolute error less than $ah_p$.
4559	A linear contraction propagates an input error without increasing it.
4560	For a bilinear contraction $\mathcal M$, replacing its operands gives
4561	\[
4562	 \|\mathcal M(f',g')-\mathcal M(f,g)\|
4563	 \le \|f'-f\|\,\|g'\|+\|f\|\,\|g'-g\|.
4564	\]
4565	When all four operands are in the disk, their two errors therefore add.
4566	
4567	We also need the norm as well as the error of a computed phase product.
4568	Let $e$ be a unit phase, let $\widetilde e$ be a disk-grid approximation
4569	with $|\widetilde e-e|<2h_p$, and let $x$ be a disk operand.  The
4570	truncation bound in \eqref{eq:transform-truncate} gives
4571	\[
4572	 \|Q_p(\widetilde e x)-ex\|
4573	   <(2\|x\|+\sqrt2)h_p<4h_p,
4574	 \qquad
4575	 \|Q_p(\widetilde e x)\|\le\|x\|.
4576	\]
4577	The second inequality follows from $|\widetilde e|\le1$ and the fact
4578	that $Q_p$ does not increase the norm.  It preserves every smaller
4579	operand norm through a twist or an endpoint phase multiplication.
4580	The same bounds hold coordinatewise for arrays of phases.
4581	
4582	For disk-grid ring arrays $f,g$, put $M=T/r$.  Two normalized synthetic
4583	forwards, pointwise polynomial multiplication divided by $r$, and the
4584	normalized opposite transform give $(f*g)/(rM^2)$.  The exact
4585	multiplication by $M$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:synthetic-convolution}
4586	then gives $\mathcal M_r(f,g)=(f*g)/T$.  Before that multiplication,
4587	the three transform errors and the polynomial-product truncation total
4588	less than $3L+2$.  Thus the error of the returned normalized
4589	convolution is bounded by
4590	\[
4591	 E_{\rm ring}:=M(3L+2)<5TL.
4592	\]
4593	If one operand has norm at most $.7$, bilinear contraction gives
4594	$\|\mathcal M_r(f,g)\|\le.7$.  Its computed grid output consequently
4595	has norm less than $.7+5TLh_p<.701$ for large $n$.  This proves the
4596	disk margin after the scale $M$, without clipping the output.
4597	
4598	Consider now $\widetilde{\mathcal M}_{\mathbb C}(f,g)$ for disk grid
4599	operands, one of norm at most $.7$.  Its two computed input twists
4600	$f',g'$ are disk grid arrays, and the smaller one still has norm at
4601	most $.7$ by the phase inequality.  The identification $\iota$
4602	preserves these bounds.  The preceding ring margin therefore gives
4603	$\|h'\|<.701$.  Neither $\iota^{-1}$ nor the computed output untwist
4604	increases this norm.  In particular,
4605	$\widetilde{\mathcal M}_{\mathbb C}(f,g)$ is a disk grid array.

4855	any remaining fixed power of $\log p$.

4857	Here $d^2$ is absorbed by $d^2\ell^\tau$, and
4858	$\log(rp)=O(p^{1-\epsilon}+\log p)=O(p^{1-\epsilon})$.

4861	individual butterfly rounds in Lemma~\ref{lem:synthetic-transform-cost}
4862	use $O(dK)$ linear scans. Its positional layout uses $O(p/K)$ exchanges
4863	of width-$K$ chunks, because $d\ell=O(p)$. Each exchange costs
4864	$O(VK^\tau)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:chunk-swap}, so the normalized total is
4865	\[
4866	 O(p/K)\,K^\tau=O(pK^{\tau-1}).
4867	\]

4869	Proposition~\ref{prop:simultaneous-layer} supplies $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$

4875	Each costs $O(V(1+\ell^\tau))$: peel a single excess bit when widths
4876	differ by one, exchange their equal-width parts, and restore the bit.

4892	sums of $d$ terms $s_i j_i^2(r/t_i)$.  Computing their squares and

4894	on $N$-bit inputs,

4897	they use a fixed number of exact products on $O(p)$-bit component
4898	numerators, followed by linear truncation scans.  The two final products
4899	by $S$ also cost $O(p\log p)$ per entry, so their normalized cost is

4901	polynomial records in each pointwise ring product.  Four integer
4902	products on $O(rp)$ bits per record therefore cost
4903	$O(Tp\log(rp))$ in total.  Signed packing, centered extraction,
4904	negacyclic wrapping, and copying are linear stream passes.  These calls
4905	use the previously established multiplier on records of length
4906	$O(rp)=o(n)$; they do not call the improved algorithm being constructed.
4907	The exact source scaling by $2^\gamma$ is a shift of $O(p)$-bit
4908	numerators by $\gamma=O(p)$ places, so it is a linear scan per entry
4909	and fits the final-scaling row. The scalar-format adapters and the exact
4910	removal of sign-extension bits after the ring and source scales also use
4911	linear scans of their $O(p)$-bit components, within the listed scan costs.

4913	\paragraph{Setup and exceptional streams across all calls.}
4914	We next separate setup at recursion nodes from work repeated for every
4915	polynomial record or every Gaussian line.  Here a visit means a node
4916	of the layer or address-layout recursions, or one of their round and
4917	group invocations.  The internal recursion of the established integer
4918	multiplier and the iterations of the quoted Gaussian algorithms are
4919	already included in their separately charged running times.
4920	The layer and address-layout recursions have constant branching and
4921	depth $O(\log p)$, and the number of their rounds and base-$m$ groups
4922	is polynomial in $p$.  Choose a fixed exponent $A$ so that their
4923	total number of visits is at most $p^A$, and a fixed $C$ bounding
4924	descriptor setup performed once per visit by $p^C$ steps.  This setup then
4925	costs at most $p^{A+C}=o(Tp)$.
4926	
4927	At a layer or synthetic-transform visit that processes polynomial
4928	records, there are at most $O(T/r)$ such records, including the
4929	bounded row padding.  Every relevant child keeps the whole
4930	length-$r$ polynomial suffix.  Consequently $O(p^C)$ descriptor or
4931	address work per record, over these visits, costs at most
4932	$O(Tp^{A+C}/r)=o(Tp)$.  Setup before each Gaussian line call has a
4933	different count:
4934	there are at most $2dT/r$ lines per tensor map and only a fixed number
4935	of such maps, so $O(p^C)$ setup per line costs
4936	$O(dTp^C/r)=o(Tp)$.  These estimates all use that $r$ exceeds every
4937	fixed power of $p$.

4939	The general address-swap subroutine also covers one-bit payloads,
4940	where no polynomial suffix is available. For root volume $V_0$ and
4941	current child volume $V_j$, the descriptor estimate in the proof of
4942	Proposition~\ref{prop:power-interchange} gives
4943	$(\log(2V_0))^{O(1)}=O(V_j)$. It uses the invariant that both original
4944	chunk ranges remain present in every child, and therefore includes
4945	polynomial descriptor work even for a one-bit payload.
4946	Elementary counter updates use local length copies, so they do not
4947	rescan a growing descriptor for each data bit.  The chirp computation
4948	does scan the axis descriptors at every coefficient; its
4949	$O(Tdp^{1+\delta})$ cost was included in the chirp row.

4951	For one packed change of basis, let $V_{\rm call}$ be its current
4952	logical volume.  The bad-address fraction is
4953	$O(d2^{-K})$, independently of the payload.  Each polynomial record
4954	has $\Theta(rp)$ payload bits, and an exceptional record adds an
4955	$O(p)$-bit destination key.  Thus the compact exceptional stream has
4956	length
4957	\[
4958	 O\!\left(\frac{V_{\rm call}}{rp}\,d2^{-K}(rp+p)\right)
4959	   =O(V_{\rm call}d2^{-K}).
4960	\]

4962	cost $O(V_{\rm call}dp2^{-K})$.  Extraction and reinsertion use a
4963	constant number of scans of the full current volume; those scans are
4964	already in the node overhead.  Since there are at most $p^A$ visits,
4965	each of volume $O(V)$, the compact sorting costs sum to at most
4966	\[
4967	 O\!\left(dp2^{-K}\sum_{\rm calls}V_{\rm call}\right)
4968	   =O(Vp^{A'}2^{-K})=o(V)
4969	\]
4970	for another fixed exponent $A'$.  Here $d=O(p^\epsilon)$ and
4971	$K=\Theta(p^{\epsilon c})$ with $\epsilon c>0$.  Predicate and key
4972	arithmetic is the polynomial work per record counted above.  This is
4973	a deterministic worst-case bound.

4976	families.  A child parks and restores only its parent's streams, with
4977	the stack head at the active top; copying and cleanup are charged to
4978	that logical volume.  No operation repeatedly scans parked ancestors.
4979	Growing axis lists and call states are stored data, not extra tapes or
4980	alphabet symbols.  Global setup and prime search cost $o(V)$, as
4981	proved earlier.

4983	Each of the seven displayed powers is at most $1-2\kappa$ by
4984	\eqref{eq:margin-list}.  Any fixed power of $\log p$ is at most $p^\kappa$
4985	eventually.  The complete large-input bound is consequently
4986	\[
4987	 O(Tp\,p^{1-\kappa})=O(n(\log n)^{1-\kappa}).
4988	\]
4989	Fix one cutoff beyond all the size, precision, margin and layout

4991	many smaller lengths are included by enlarging the implicit constant.

4994	$O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ for every input length and produces precisely

The procedure constructs an explicit positional
layout permutation $L$ of record addresses, preserving their polynomial
suffixes, and transforms disk grid arrays of $M$ contiguous
degree-less-than-$r$ polynomial records. Its exact counterpart is
$LB F_{\boldsymbol t}^-$.  Its opposite procedure consumes

$F_{\boldsymbol t}^+B^{-1}L^{-1}$.  Each procedure has error less than

Both layout construction and final restoration are charged in this
bound.  The forward procedure may retain its output layout for a
pointwise product and the following opposite procedure.

\begin{proof}
Put $D=d-1$ and write $a_i=\log_2t_i$. The supplied encoding has
$2w=\Theta(p)$ bits per coefficient, so the logical bit volume is
$\Theta(Tp)$.  Call an axis long if $a_i=\ell$ and short if
$a_i=\ell-1$.  Name the original bit slots of axis $i$ by
$(i,h)$, $a_i-1\geq h\geq0$.  Initially these slots are in axis order
and, within each axis, in decreasing $h$.  The coefficients of each
polynomial form a contiguous suffix.  Put
\[
       b=(\ell-1)\bmod K,
       \qquad q=\lfloor(\ell-1)/K\rfloor.
\]
Form a list of the slots to move to a prefix.  First list
$(i,\ell-1)$ for the length-$2^\ell$ axes in increasing $i$.
Then list $(i,h)$ for $h=b-1,\ldots,0$, and within each $h$ in
increasing $i$; this second list is empty if $b=0$.  Move each listed
slot immediately after the prefix already formed, leaving all other
slots in their relative order.  There are at most $D(b+1)=O(dK)$
listed slots, so the moves cost $O(TpdK)$.  A descriptor records the
physical position of every named slot.  The part of each axis left
outside the prefix now consists of $q$ consecutive $K$-bit chunks.

\subsection{Chirp and source-transform procedures}

We next use the complex convolution to evaluate the middle factor
$QF_{\boldsymbol t}$ in \eqref{eq:no-sort-tensor}, and then compose it
with the Gaussian maps. For the chirp array $a$ in
\eqref{eq:permuted-chirp}, the phase numerator
at tensor address $j$ is computed modulo $2r$ as
\[
 -\sum_i s_i j_i^2(r/t_i)\pmod{2r}.
\]
All integers have $O(p)$ bits and $r/t_i\in\{1,2\}$.  Scan the stored
axis descriptors and compute the $d$ squares and products with the
previously established integer multiplier.  Additions, reductions
modulo a power of two, and restarting local counters cost $O(p)$ per
term; multiplication costs $O(p\log p)=O(p^{1+\delta})$.  Exponential
evaluation then has the same $O(p^{1+\delta})$ bound.  Thus chirp
------
Lemma~\ref{lem:chirp-permutation}, applied to
$U=RF_{\boldsymbol s}u$ and $V_1=RF_{\boldsymbol s}v$, gives
\[
 G(U\cdot V_1)=(u*v)/S^2.
\]
The computed opposite transform may be applied to $z$ because
$\|z\|<.5$. Insert $G$ at that computed input:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|\widetilde{\mathscr F}^{+}(z)-G(U\cdot V_1)\|
 &\le \|\widetilde{\mathscr F}^{+}(z)-Gz\|\\
 &\qquad+\|G(z-U\cdot V_1)\|\\
 &<(3E_s+2)h_p.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first exact numerator multiplication by $S$ gives
$\widetilde w$, approximating $w=(u*v)/S$ with error less than
$E_wh_p$, where
\[
 E_w:=S(3E_s+2)<28\,2^\gamma T^2L.
\]
Each coefficient of $w$ is an average of $S$ products of coefficients
of $u$ and $v$, so $\|w\|<1/16$.  The earlier cutoff therefore gives
\[
 \|\widetilde w\|<1/16+E_wh_p<1/16+10^{-3}<1.
\]
This proves the disk bound for the computed first scaled result.

In tensor order, the unscaled integer coefficient array is
$2^{2b+4}S w$.  This second occurrence of $S$ reverses the
normalization still present in $w$, and $2^{2b+4}$ reverses the two
input scales.  Both multiplications act exactly on grid numerators.
Since $S\le T<2^b$ and $L<b$ eventually, the final absolute error is less than
\begin{equation}\label{eq:final-error}
 2^{2b+4}S\cdot28\,2^\gamma T^2L\cdot2^{-6b}
 <448b\,2^{-b+\gamma}
 \le448b\,2^{-3b/4}<\frac12.
\end{equation}
The true coefficients are real integers.  If $H_j$ is the real
numerator after the second scaling, its represented value is
$H_j/2^p$.  The strict error below $1/2$ makes the nearest integer to
that value the unique correct coefficient.

These exact operations use known fixed record widths. If $N$ is a
signed $w_0$-bit integer, then $-2^{w_0-1}\leq N<2^{w_0-1}$. Since
$0<S<2^b$, its product satisfies
$-2^{w_0+b-1}<SN<2^{w_0+b-1}$ and therefore fits in signed width $w_0+b$.
The first product by $S$ starts at width $w_{\rm c}$ and is written in
width $w_{\rm c}+b$. The next product by $S$ is written in width
$w_{\rm c}+2b$; appending $2b+4$ least significant zero bits then gives
the exact second scale in width $w_{\rm c}+4b+4$. Each complex record
still places its most-significant-bit-first real word before its imaginary
word. The known widths determine every boundary in the next scan and are
$O(p)$ because $p=6b$.

The established integer multiplier performs the two products by $S$ in
$O(p\log p)$ time per entry. To serialize each exact signed product at
its stated width, zero-pad its magnitude and complement and increment
for a negative sign. The proved bounds ensure that no significant bit is
discarded. These conversions and the power-of-two shift use linear scans.
To round $H_j/2^p$, recover the real magnitude, inspect its low $p$ bits,
and apply the rounding carry with the sign restored. The strict error
bound makes the result the correct nonnegative coefficient, and
\eqref{eq:capacity} puts it in $[0,2^{3b})$. It therefore fits in one
signed $(3b+1)$-bit two's-complement word, written most significant bit
first. Scan the padded box in the
physical axis order recorded by its shape descriptor, using the same
$O(p)$-bit nested counters and validity tests as above. Consume the
imaginary word and write this real coefficient word at each valid address,
with an all-zero
word at each padded address. This serialization costs $O(Tp)$ in total.

u&\leftarrow&u-c[\,w\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(1)\\
w&\leftarrow&w-c[\,u\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(2)\\
u&\leftarrow&u+c[\,w\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(3)\\
w&\leftarrow&w+c[\,u\equiv0\pmod2\,],&(4)\\

u&\leftarrow&u-c[\,w\equiv1\pmod2\,].&(8)
\end{array}
\end{equation}
If $c=0$, these operations do nothing. If $c=1$, the first four operations
induce the cycle $(00\ 01\ 10)$ in every square
\[
 \{2a,2a+1\}\times\{2b,2b+1\},\qquad a,b\in\mathbb Z,
\]
where the corner labels record the parities of $(u,w)$. The last four
induce $(01\ 10\ 11)$. Applying the first cycle and then the second gives
$(00\ 10)(01\ 11)$. These facts follow by substituting the four parity
pairs into the displayed operations; translation by $(2a,2b)$ does not
change any predicate. Consequently the complete output is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eight-packed-result}
 (u',w')=
 \bigl(u+c(1-2(u\bmod2)),\ w\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here $u\bmod2\in\{0,1\}$, also for negative $u$. Thus the parity of $u$
is flipped precisely when $c=1$, both quotients under division by two are
preserved, and the arbitrary auxiliary integer $w$ is restored. Each
coordinate is updated four times by at most one, so its displacement
from its initial value is at most four, even if an intermediate point
leaves its starting quotient square. The weaker bound eight will suffice below.

Omit the most significant selected position $j_{f-1}$ temporarily. For
each $0\le i<f-1$, the bits in positions
$j_i,\ldots,j_i+K-1$ form a $K$-bit segment. When $f>1$, these segments
are disjoint, and the highest one ends immediately below $j_{f-1}$.
Write their initial values in $y$ and $z$ as
\[
 u_i=2g_i+a_i,\qquad w_i=2h_i+b_i,
 \qquad a_i,b_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The values $g_i,h_i\in\{0,\ldots,2^{K-1}-1\}$ are the guard values. The
control for this pair of segments is the selected bit $c_i=x_{j_i}$.

Apply each line of \eqref{eq:eight-packed-additions} simultaneously to all
these segment pairs. Physically, a line updating $y$ by sign $\varepsilon$
and testing parity $b$ of $z$ is the single cyclic shift
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:packed-cyclic-shift}
 y\longleftarrow y+
 \varepsilon\sum_{i=0}^{f-2}2^{j_i}
 [\,x_{j_i}=1\,][\,z_{j_i}=b\,]
 \pmod{2^L}.
\end{equation}
For a line updating $z$, interchange $y$ and $z$ in this formula.
The shift offset never depends on its target chunk, so each line is a
bijection of the rectangle. Let $S_0$ be their composition. It fixes
the spectator coordinates.
